title: WHO Guidelines for medicine donations: what applies to every destination
notes: WHO, Guidelines for medicine donations, revised 2010 (ISBN 978 92 4 150198 9), section 3, articles 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11 and 12, and section 4. Read by Claude on 2026-11-17 from the PDF linked on the publication page (SHA-256 cb41c017c38714425150f3e82f7d12b72667ae3c5192207b996723dc088cb89b, the same file as the shelf-life rule). Verified by the owner item by item against the PDF on 2026-11-17 (REV-013, ADR-045). Each item restates its article; exceptions are given as notes in the guideline's words. Rule cards never print 'approved' or 'clearance' (SYS-309, ADR-044), so 'approved for use' (article 2) is written 'authorised for use', 'port clearance' (article 12) 'port and customs storage and handling', and 'customs clearance' (section 4) 'getting the shipment through customs'. Article 7's 'In the case of injections, the route of administration should be indicated' is left out because injections are out of scope in this build (ADR-010). Section 4's guidance on labelling for pregnancy, children and other conditions ('where appropriate and whenever possible') is not included. Verified for the prototype (OD-006, ADR-022); external review by a pharmacist or clinician is still needed before real-world use (OD-002), as are each country's own rules (OD-003).

items.requirement: The donation is based on an expressed need of the recipient and is relevant to the disease pattern in the recipient country; the quantities are agreed between donor and recipient; and the medicines are not sent without the recipient's prior consent (articles 1 and 10).
items.note: Exception (article 1): in acute emergencies, the need for prior consent by the recipient may be waived, provided that the medicines are among those on the WHO model lists of essential medicines or are included in the United Nations list of emergency relief items recommended for use in acute emergencies.

items.requirement: Each medicine, or its generic equivalent, is authorised for use in the recipient country and appears on the national list of essential medicines or equivalent, or in the national standard treatment guidelines if that list is not updated; or, if there is no national list, on the WHO model lists of essential medicines, unless the recipient asks otherwise and gives a reason (article 2).
items.note: Exception (article 2): medicines needed in sudden outbreaks of uncommon or newly emerging diseases, provided the donor informs the recipient of each product's regulatory status and obtains the recipient's agreement.

items.requirement: Each medicine comes from a quality-ensured source, is authorised for sale in the country of origin, is made to good manufacturing practice (GMP), and meets quality standards in both the donor and the recipient country; the WHO Certification Scheme on the Quality of Pharmaceutical Products Moving in International Commerce is used (article 4; documents, section 4).
items.document: Documents proving compliance with quality standards
items.note: Exception (article 4): in acute emergencies, where pre-stock or the emergency health kit are not in place, the WHO Certification Scheme may not be practical; if it is not used, the donor gives a solid justification.

items.requirement: No medicine has been issued to patients and then returned, or given to health professionals as a free sample (article 5).
After arrival in the recipient country, each medicine has a remaining shelf life of at least one year, and the quantities donated match what can be used before they expire (article 6).
items.note: Prepped checks one year as 365 days from the arrival date (ADR-013). Not applied in this build (OD-053): the exceptions for direct donations to a specific health facility and for medicines with a total shelf life of less than two years, and a national donation policy's own minimum (article 6).

items.requirement: Each container is labelled in a language easily understood by health professionals in the recipient country, with at least the International Nonproprietary Name (INN) or generic name, batch number, dosage form, strength, name of manufacturer, country of manufacture, quantity in the container, storage conditions and expiry date (article 7).

The shipment is packed to international shipping requirements with a detailed packing list of the contents; each carton preferably weighs no more than 30 kilograms; and medicines are not mixed with other supplies, unless they are shipped as kits with predetermined contents (article 9).
The declared value is based on the wholesale price of the generic equivalent in the recipient country, or else the wholesale world-market price (article 11).
items.note: Exception (article 11): for patented medicines with no generic equivalent, the wholesale price of the nearest therapeutic equivalent could be taken as a reference.

items.requirement: The donor pays the costs of international and local transport, warehousing, port and customs storage and handling, and disposal or return of expired donated products, unless agreed otherwise with the recipient in advance (article 12).

Roles and responsibilities for transport, getting the shipment through customs, reception, storage and distribution, administration, monitoring and evaluation and, where warranted, disposal of the donated medicines are agreed in writing and signed by the donor and the recipient before the medicines arrive (section 4).
items.document: Signed agreement on roles and responsibilities
